summary: Discovery focused on consolidating multiple model providers into a single inference platform. Customer currently uses OpenAI for chat, a self-hosted vLLM stack for cost-sensitive workloads, and Azure-managed endpoints for regulated data. Major blockers: VPC/on-prem requirements, KMS integration, eval parity with existing models (especially TGI/vLLM artifacts), and predictable latency/SLOs. AE+SE outlined Redwood hosted, Dedicated, and Private options and proposed a PoC to validate latency and quality parity using customer's prompt set.
topics: Migration strategy from OpenAI/Anthropic to Redwood
Performance: latency SLOs, KV cache, batching
transcript:
Meeting Header: Date: 2026-07-28 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jonah Rivera (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Phoenix DataOps Head of ML), Samir Patel (Infra Lead), Rachel Kim (Procurement), Andre Yu (SRE), Priya Desai (ML Engineer)

Summary (auto): Customer evaluating consolidation of multiple inference providers. Primary concerns: security/compliance, model/eval parity, and predictable latency at 99th percentile. Proposed next step: PoC using their prompt set and parallel benchmarking.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, I think we are looking at about 45 minutes, is that still good?
[00:05] Lena Ortiz: Yes, perfect. We have Samir, Rachel, Andre and Priya on the line. We'll try to keep questions high level first then go deep.
[00:12] Maya Chen: Great. Quick intro: I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and Jonah is our SE who'll take most of the tech questions. Quick goal for the call: where you're at with OpenAI/Anthropic/vLLM today, what blockers you have, and discuss hosted vs dedicated vs private options.
[00:28] Jonah Rivera: Hi all. Also to note, we work a lot on latency and cost tradeoffs so we'll ask about token distributions and throughput.
[00:35] Lena Ortiz: Cool. So brief background: Phoenix DataOps runs customer-facing chat on OpenAI right now, internal long-form generation on a vLLM cluster, and some sensitive regs stuff on Azure managed endpoints. We're looking to consolidate to reduce vendor sprawl and cut per-token spend while keeping quality.
[00:55] Samir Patel: Also from infra, our SRE team wants predictable 99th percentile latency, and we need VPC access or on-prem for some clients in finance.
[01:05] Jonah Rivera: Makes sense. Quick clarifying question: when you say vLLM cluster, are you using the open-source vLLM stack with Triton or custom runtime?
[01:12] Priya Desai: It's a mix — vLLM open stack running on a fleet of A100s with some custom TGI adapters we wrote for multi-turn context.
[01:20] Jonah Rivera: Okay that helps. Two immediate areas we usually look at: binary/model compatibility and inference behavior parity. When you mention TGI adapters, do you have model forks or custom tokenizers?
[01:30] Priya Desai: We have a small fork for tokenizer handling multi-lingual prompts and some temperature scheduling logic, but nothing too crazy.
[01:38] Maya Chen: Good — that usually maps well to our model onboarding. For compatibility, Redwood supports common transformer checkpoints and we have an onboarding path for TGI/vLLM artifacts; sometimes tokenization quirks require small token-mapper layers.
[01:50] Lena Ortiz: The big concern though is eval parity. If we move to Redwood hosted or dedicated we need to see identical or near-identical outputs for our existing prompts and a way to run continuous evals.
[01:58] Jonah Rivera: Totally. For PoC we typically run side-by-side inference: you give us the prompt corpus, we run it on your vLLM/TGI baseline and on Redwood hosted/dedicated/private variants, and compare metrics: exact-match, bleu-ish scores, embedding similarity, and business KPIs.
[02:12] Samir Patel: What's the overhead to spin up a dedicated pool? We have burst patterns where nightly batch jobs spike tokens a lot.
[02:18] Maya Chen: Dedicated is a reserved GPU pool; you can configure autoscaling with burst capacity. Pricing-wise it'd be a commit + overage model. For burst we can attach temporary burst capacity in hosted to cover peaks while you scale dedicated.
[02:30] Rachel Kim: From procurement: timeline — we usually need 30 days for contracts and an enterprise security review. Do you have SOC2 / ISO docs?
[02:38] Jonah Rivera: Yes, we provide SOC2 and ISO 27001 reports, and we can do an NDA and SSO/SAML integration. For Private deployments we support customer KMS/HSM integrations.
[02:48] Andre Yu: Important: our compliance team requires audit logs at token-level for certain datasets; is that available?
[02:54] Maya Chen: We can provide detailed request/response logs and token-level cost breakdowns in Redwood Console, and for Private we can route logs to your SIEM with S3/CLS ingestion.
[03:08] Lena Ortiz: Good. One technical worry: our vLLM stack uses KV cache for multi-turn acceleration. How does Redwood handle KV caching and warm starts?
[03:16] Jonah Rivera: Redwood runtime supports KV cache semantics and we have prefix caching and TTL-based hot cache. For dedicated/private you can pin models with warmed cache snapshots to reduce cold-starts. Sometimes the exact in-memory cache format differs, but we expose an API for cache snapshots/restore during PoC.
[03:30] Priya Desai: Any gotchas with quantization? We've been running int8 on some models to save cost.
[03:36] Jonah Rivera: We support quantized variants and recommend quantization profiles per workload. The main tradeoff is slight output variance at certain temp/decoding settings — part of the PoC is to measure that.
[03:48] Samir Patel: Network topology question: for Private do you manage the control plane? We need the data plane in VPC and control plane minimal exposure.
[03:56] Maya Chen: Private keeps the control plane in our cloud but can be configured to talk over private connectivity and we also offer a customer-managed control plane for air-gapped installs in specific enterprise deals.
[04:08] Lena Ortiz: Let's talk numbers: our peak interactive workload is about 250 qps with 1.2k avg tokens per request, but we also have nightly batch at 3k qps for embeddings. Cost sensitivity is high.
[04:20] Jonah Rivera: Helpful. We'll size for 250 rps interactive and a separate batch queue; batching and caching strategies differ. For embeddings at scale we often recommend dedicated pools with optimized GPU types for throughput.
[04:30] Maya Chen: Also latency SLO: what's acceptable 99th?
[04:34] Samir Patel: We need 99th under 600ms for interactive. Batch can be higher.
[04:38] Jonah Rivera: 600ms 99th for that token count is challenging on shared hosted if you need consistency. Dedicated with tuned batching and caching and locality typically meets that; Private on-prem gives most control but adds integration overhead.
[04:50] Lena Ortiz: Are there customers who moved from vLLM to Redwood and kept eval parity?
[04:54] Maya Chen: Yes — we did a migration with a fintech customer that had custom tokenizers. It required a tokenizer adapter and a small rerun of their eval suite; parity was within acceptable thresholds for their KPIs. We'll share a short case note.
[05:06] Rachel Kim: On contract terms: do you require a minimum commitment for Dedicated?
[05:10] Maya Chen: Yes typically monthly or annual commitments, but flexible pilots are possible with temporary credits.
[05:15] Priya Desai: If we run a PoC, can we keep our vLLM cluster running side-by-side and compare A/B?
[05:20] Jonah Rivera: Absolutely — side-by-side A/B is the usual approach. We can instrument and produce metrics and diffs.
[05:26] Andre Yu: Security deep dive later: we want to validate KMS integration and HSM rotations.
[05:30] Maya Chen: Noted, we can have a dedicated security review with our security engineer.
[05:34] Lena Ortiz: Ok, let's outline success criteria: 1) parity on core prompt set within X% similarity, 2) 99th < 600ms for interactive, 3) predictable token cost improvement of at least 20% for batch workloads.
[05:46] Maya Chen: Those are crisp, we can build the PoC to target those.
[05:50] Jonah Rivera: For the PoC plan: you provide the prompt set and token distribution; we run the baseline on your vLLM/TGI infra and run Redwood hosted/dedicated/private variants. We'll produce a report with latency percentiles, output diffs, and cost delta.
[06:06] Samir Patel: How long does onboarding take? We have one sprint to prepare assets.
[06:10] Maya Chen: For a basic PoC usually 2-3 weeks from kickoff, depending on availability and complexity of tokenizer/model forks. If there are heavier infra hooks for Private, add another week.
[06:20] Rachel Kim: Can you send a templated SOW for PoC that we can review?
[06:24] Maya Chen: Yes, I'll send a PoC SOW + pricing and the security docs.
[06:28] Lena Ortiz: A few technical nitty-gritty: our multi-turn context uses custom state passing; do you support function/tool-calling style IO?
[06:36] Jonah Rivera: We support structured outputs and function-calling patterns and can map your state pass into our session API. We might need a small shim if your format is unconventional.
[06:46] Priya Desai: We also use a home-grown prompt templating layer that injects external KB. We need to ensure latency to embeddings store doesn't blow the SLOs.
[06:54] Maya Chen: That's a perfect use-case for caching embeddings at the request layer; Redwood Console has tracing so you can see end-to-end latency attribution.
[07:04] Lena Ortiz: Any gotchas when moving from Anthropic models? We use Anthropic for safety reasons in some flows.
[07:12] Jonah Rivera: Safety guardrails are part technical, part policy. We can host safety-tuned models and integrate policy layers; sometimes the prompt-engineered behaviors differ and require iterative calibration. For regulated flows we recommend Private with fine-grained rollout control.
[07:26] Samir Patel: What about model updates and rollouts? We need canary and A/B.
[07:30] Maya Chen: Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B traffic splits, and automatic fallback to a previous model if errors increase.
[07:38] Lena Ortiz: Suppose we want the control plane onsite — is that doable?
[07:42] Jonah Rivera: In enterprise agreements we can provide a customer-managed control plane or an on-prem bundle; that requires procurement and security sign-off but it's supported.
[07:52] Rachel Kim: Ok procurement note: send pricing bands for hosted/dedicated/private and the typical contract lead times.
[07:58] Maya Chen: Will do.
[08:00] -- brief pause, background noise --
[08:10] Priya Desai: A quick technical question: does Redwood expose raw logits or token probabilities for our RL evaluation?
[08:16] Jonah Rivera: Yes, we can expose token-level logits / probabilities in the debug traces for PoC, though for hosted we might have a gated export depending on privacy constraints. For Private it's fully available.
[08:28] Andre Yu: For our nightly embedding jobs, how do you recommend handling cold-start vs warm cache across many small tenants?
[08:36] Jonah Rivera: For multi-tenant batch, we recommend persistent embedding workers with pre-warmed model instances and prioritized batch queues. Also shard embeddings pools by model size to avoid noisy neighbors.
[08:48] Lena Ortiz: Alright, this is helpful. Anything else we should cover?
[08:52] Maya Chen: One last thing — pricing for embeddings vs text gen can differ; we'll lay out cost-per-1k tokens and embedding per 1k vectors. Also include estimated savings for quantized dedicated setups.
[09:06] Rachel Kim: Please also include a sample SLA for Dedicated.
[09:10] Maya Chen: We'll include a sample SLA and uptime numbers.
[09:12] Lena Ortiz: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[09:16] Maya Chen: Recap: Maya sends PoC SOW + pricing + security pack by 7/30; Jonah runs initial latency sim and shares by 8/03; Lena shares prompt set and token distribution by 7/31; Rachel coordinates procurement timeline and confirms PO process by 8/05.
[09:32] Samir Patel: We'll also want to schedule the security deep-dive with your sec engineer.
[09:36] Jonah Rivera: I'll coordinate that — likely a 60-90 minute session to go over KMS, audit logs, control plane options.
[09:44] Lena Ortiz: Thanks everyone.
[09:46] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and the attachments.
[09:50] -- meeting ends --

Notes: Transcript contains typical ASR noise; attendee labels may be generic in spots. References to vLLM/TGI may appear as v LLM or T G I in the transcript.
